D1 research authoring, batch 84 (2026-09-27): two ASSOCIATION_ONLY draft mappings added at ranks 1-2 (sialadenitis, xerostomia) pending qualified-human citation verification under docs/citation-verification-sop.md; mapping approval is not citation verification. Rank order follows the strength of the located evidence rather than clinical sequence: the sialadenitis edge is ranked first because it is the defining clinical event of the identity, while the xerostomia edge is ranked second because the located evidence for it contains an explicit negative result.

Classification guard: both edges assert documented association only, with MECHANICAL_OR_COMPRESSIVE named as the shared vector and the reversibility of the dryness explicitly distinguished from the permanent acinar loss of an autoimmune sicca state, so neither edge may be read as asserting gland destruction.

Both edges require the competing obstructive and systemic aetiologies named by the located rapid evidence review to be excluded by name, namely dehydration, malnutrition, medication effect, chronic systemic illness, ductal stenosis, trauma and mucocele, because the located evidence attributes salivary stasis and inflammation to those alternatives as well.

nexusClaim.associationBasis: A salivary calculus obstructs its duct, and the obstructed gland is the recognised site of the secondary inflammation that defines the obstructive sialadenitis presentation. A rapid evidence review of salivary gland disorders states that sialolithiasis causes up to 50 percent of salivary gland disorders, that the submandibular glands, whose mucinous secretions are high in calcium and phosphate salts and which drain through a long duct that flows against gravity, are responsible for MORE THAN 80 PERCENT OF SALIVARY STONES, and that sialolithiasis IS ASSOCIATED WITH SALIVARY STASIS AND INFLAMMATION caused by dehydration, malnutrition, medications or chronic illness, with obstruction also caused by trauma, stenosis and mucoceles (PMID 38905553). A monograph chapter reviewing the three most frequently diagnosed salivary gland diseases states that sialolithiasis is characterized by calcified structures developing in the salivary glands, especially the submandibular gland, that SIALOLITHS ARE GENERALLY ATTRIBUTED TO RETENTION OF SALIVA, and that they are usually accompanied by swelling and pain when a salivary stimulus is applied (PMID 24862601). A prospective cohort of 41 patients with sialolithiasis obstructive sialadenitis, who were expressly EXCLUDED if they had acute sialadenitis, showed whole-saliva sialometry improving from 2.21 to 3.42 g for the submandibular gland and from 1.87 to 2.92 g for the parotid at 12 months after gland-sparing sialolithotomy, and a parallel improvement in the Multidisciplinary Salivary Gland Society quality-of-life score from 65.92 to 3.84 for the submandibular gland, which is the functional signature of a stone-driven process that reverses when the stone is removed (PMID 41213527). Recorded as documented association only, with the third anchor's treatment-outcome design carried openly.
nexusClaim.causationStatus: Neither causation nor aggravation is established for any individual, and the honest position is that this is the most mechanistically obvious route in the batch while resting on the weakest anchor class in it. Two of the three anchors are narrative syntheses rather than primary data: the rapid evidence review asserts the association with stasis and inflammation without reporting an incidence, and the monograph chapter attributes calculi to saliva retention and describes the meal-related swelling and pain without a cohort (PMID 38905553, PMID 24862601). The one primary anchor is a single-arm treatment-outcome cohort of 41 patients whose salivary function RECOVERED AFTER STONE REMOVAL, which is strong functional evidence that the stone drives the dysfunction but is a before-and-after design in all of whom the intervention was performed, and the authors did not randomise or include a comparator, so regression to the mean, natural resolution of intermittent obstruction, and the sialendoscopy procedure itself are not separable from the stone (PMID 41213527). Individual claims require a dated sialolithiasis diagnosis with imaging confirmation of a calculus, a dated sialadenitis diagnosis with documented gland swelling and its relationship to meals, and a documented exclusion of the competing causes the located review names, namely dehydration, malnutrition, medication effect, chronic systemic illness, ductal stenosis, trauma and mucoceles, because the located evidence explicitly attributes stasis and inflammation to those alternatives as well.

causalMechanism.primaryVector: The hypothesised vector is mechanical obstruction of a salivary excretory duct by a calculus, which arrests the normal anterograde flow of saliva and produces upstream stasis, and in which the stagnant, pooled secretion behind an obstructed duct becomes the substrate for ascending bacterial infection, so that a retained stone converts a self-limiting obstruction into recurrent or chronic gland inflammation. The vector is named as obstruction-then-stasis-then-infection rather than as a direct stone-to-tissue effect because the located evidence describes calculi as attributed to retention of saliva rather than as irritants in their own right, and because the located rapid evidence review locates the inflammation in the stasis and its causes rather than in the calculus itself, which is why the alternative aetiologies are named rather than treated as incidental.

evidentiaryProfile.conservativeRationale: Authored at ASSOCIATION_ONLY at rapid-evidence-review, monograph-chapter, and prospective-cohort class. The rapid evidence review is the anchor that supplies the epidemiologic framing, sialolithiasis accounting for up to 50 percent of salivary gland disorders, the submandibular predominance above 80 percent with the mechanistic explanation of calcium and phosphate-rich mucinous secretion through a long duct that flows against gravity, and the explicit statement of the association with stasis and inflammation (PMID 38905553). The monograph chapter is the anchor that supplies the retention mechanism and the meal-related symptom pattern that is the clinical signature of obstructive disease (PMID 24862601). The prospective cohort is the anchor that supplies the QUANTITATIVE FUNCTIONAL EVIDENCE, whole-saliva recovery from 2.21 to 3.42 g after stone removal, which converts a plausible mechanism into a measured reversal and is the only primary data in this edge (PMID 41213527). Because the design evidence is narrative and the primary anchor is a single-arm intervention study, the conservative standard holds the edge at association only, names the competing obstructive and systemic aetiologies the anchors themselves list, and requires imaging confirmation plus a differential workup before any individual attribution.
evidentiaryProfile.evidenceGaps: TWO OF THE THREE ANCHORS ARE NARRATIVE SYNTHESES, not primary data, and neither reports an incidence, a risk estimate, or a comparison group, so the strength of this edge is mechanistic and clinical rather than epidemiological (PMID 38905553, PMID 24862601). The one primary anchor is a single-arm prospective cohort of 41 patients with mean age 37.88 years and 56.1 percent male, in which every patient underwent gland-sparing sialolithotomy, and its exclusions are themselves informative: patients with ACUTE SIALADENITIS WERE EXCLUDED, which means the cohort is by construction the chronic rather than the acute presentation, so the anchor cannot be used to support an acute-inflammation claim (PMID 41213527). The located chronic sialadenitis cohort that compared sialolithiasis against duct stenosis was reviewed and REJECTED as an anchor for this edge because it compares two causes of obstruction WITHIN patients who already carry a diagnosis of chronic sialadenitis, and it reports LOWER symptom burden in the sialolithiasis group than the stenosis group (SPIT 33.3 versus 45.4, P < .013), so it would have supported a claim that stones are the mildest obstructive cause rather than a claim that stones cause sialadenitis. NO located anchor reports the proportion of sialolithiasis patients who develop sialadenitis, or the proportion of sialadenitis patients whose disease is stone-driven. The xerostomia route was authored separately but is a sibling rather than a duplicate, sharing the same obstruction vector. The mucocele route was withheld as SHARED-SUBSTRATE because the located review names mucoceles among the same causes of duct obstruction, so the arrow runs toward the same obstruction from a different cause rather than from the stone.
alternativeEtiologiesToRuleOut: Ductal stenosis, which the located review names as a competing cause of obstruction and which the reviewed-but-rejected chronic sialadenitis cohort found to carry a HEAVIER symptom burden than sialolithiasis (SPIT 45.4 versus 33.3, P < .013), so it is the more likely explanation for severe obstructive sialadenitis
Dehydration, malnutrition, medication effect and chronic systemic illness, each named by the located rapid evidence review as a cause of the same salivary stasis and inflammation
Mucocele, named by the located review as a further cause of obstruction of the same excretory system
Acute suppurative sialadenitis without a stone, which the primary anchor expressly excluded from its cohort and which would present differently and more acutely

nexusClaim.associationBasis: Objective salivary gland hypofunction is a documented, measured feature of obstructive salivary disease, and it reverses when the obstruction is relieved, which is what distinguishes a stone-driven route from a permanent sicca state. A systematic review of patient-reported outcome measures for salivary function identified 16 validated instruments across 2,059 abstracts screened and 133 full texts reviewed, of which SEVEN specifically assess xerostomia, four assess sialadenitis and two assess Sjogren's syndrome, and found the Xerostomia Inventory to be the most rigorously developed instrument, rated adequate in 6 of 7 COSMIN domains, while reporting notable limitations in content validity for all included tools (PMID 36606658). A prospective cohort of 41 patients with sialolithiasis obstructive sialadenitis showed measured whole-saliva output recovering after gland-sparing stone removal, from 2.21 to 3.42 g for the submandibular gland and from 1.87 to 2.92 g for the parotid at 12 months, alongside a parallel collapse of the Multidisciplinary Salivary Gland Society quality-of-life score from 65.92 to 3.84 for the submandibular gland (PMID 41213527). A prospective non-randomised study of 37 patients undergoing sialendoscopy for benign salivary obstruction, 64.5 percent of whom had sialolithiasis, found painful swelling symptoms occurring 4.5 times per week with a symptom duration of 23.5 months on average, and 80.6 percent of the sialolithiasis clinic reporting improved symptoms after sialendoscopy (p < 0.001), together with a NEGATIVE correlation between sialendoscopy satisfaction and xerostomia (p = 0.009) (PMID 34998366). Recorded as documented association only, with the xerostomia null from the third anchor carried openly on the face of the edge.
nexusClaim.causationStatus: Neither causation nor aggravation is established for any individual, and the located evidence is genuinely split in a way that must not be smoothed over. The objective anchor is a treatment-response cohort rather than an incidence study, and its recovery figures describe gland function after relief of obstruction rather than the burden of dryness during obstruction, so it establishes that the stone drives the hypofunction without establishing how much dryness an individual stone produces (PMID 41213527). The subjective anchor is more troubling for a causal reading: although 80.6 percent of its sialolithiasis patients reported improved symptoms after sialendoscopy, the study found a NEGATIVE correlation between sialendoscopy satisfaction and xerostomia, meaning the patients whose complaint was dryness were the ones least helped, and the authors' own conclusion distinguishes a positive impact on quality of life in obstructive stone disease from a relative time-dependent indication for other causes of xerostomia that little improved satisfaction (PMID 34998366). The instrument review is a methodological systematic review of outcome measures rather than a clinical study, and it supplies the vocabulary and validated instruments rather than an effect estimate, while reporting that content validity was a notable limitation for all included tools (PMID 36606658). Individual claims therefore require a dated sialolithiasis diagnosis, a documented salivary flow measurement or a validated xerostomia instrument score with its date, a documented response to sialagogue therapy or hydration trial, and an assessment for the competing causes of dry mouth, because the located evidence shows dryness in a stone patient is frequently not what the stone explains.

causalMechanism.primaryVector: The hypothesised vector is that a calculus occluding a salivary excretory duct interrupts the delivery of saliva to the oral cavity, so that the gland continues producing secretion which has nowhere to drain, and the resulting reduction in delivered salivary volume produces the subjective sensation of oral dryness and the objective finding of reduced unstimulated and stimulated whole-saliva flow. The vector is named as obstructed delivery rather than as gland destruction, and that distinction is load-bearing: the located cohort evidence shows salivary function RECOVERING substantially after the stone is removed, so the dryness in this route is a delivery deficit that is at least partly reversible rather than the permanent acinar loss that characterises an autoimmune sicca state, which is why the autoimmune differential is named as something to exclude rather than folded in.

evidentiaryProfile.conservativeRationale: Authored at ASSOCIATION_ONLY at systematic-review, prospective-cohort, and prospective-non-randomised-study class. The instrument review is the anchor that establishes that xerostomia is a separable, measurable construct with validated instruments available, and it is the reason the edge can require a documented instrument score rather than a subjective complaint (PMID 36606658). The prospective cohort is the anchor that supplies the QUANTITATIVE FUNCTIONAL DATA, whole-saliva recovery from 2.21 to 3.42 g submandibular and 1.87 to 2.92 g parotid, and the parallel quality-of-life score collapse from 65.92 to 3.84, which is what makes the route reversible and therefore clinically meaningful (PMID 41213527). The sialendoscopy study is registered as the EXPLICIT COUNTERWEIGHT, because it reports the negative correlation between sialendoscopy satisfaction and xerostomia alongside the positive stone-clinic result, and quoting only the latter would misrepresent the evidence (PMID 34998366). Because the located evidence is split between an objective reversible deficit and a subjective complaint that the intervention often does not fix, the conservative standard holds the edge at association only, carries the null on the face of the edge, and requires both an objective and a documented subjective measure before any individual attribution.
evidentiaryProfile.evidenceGaps: The instrument review is a methodological systematic review of patient-reported outcome measures, not a clinical study, and it reports that content validity was a notable limitation for ALL of the 16 instruments it identified, none of which was rated adequate, so it supplies instruments rather than effect estimates and cannot itself support a claim about how much dryness stones cause (PMID 36606658). The primary functional anchor is a single-arm cohort of 41 patients in whom every patient underwent sialolithotomy, so the improvement cannot be separated into removal of the stone, the sialendoscopy procedure itself, regression to the mean, or the natural resolution of intermittent obstruction (PMID 41213527). The third anchor is explicitly NON-RANDOMISED and reports a NEGATIVE correlation between sialendoscopy satisfaction and xerostomia, meaning the xerostomia-specific benefit of relieving a stone is weak in exactly the patients whose principal complaint is dryness (PMID 34998366). NO located anchor reports the prevalence or measured severity of xerostomia in an untreated population of sialolithiasis patients, so the direction and magnitude of the association in the absence of intervention are unknown. This edge is ranked BELOW the sialadenitis edge because the sialadenitis relationship is the defining clinical event of the identity whereas xerostomia is one of its manifestations, and because the located evidence for the dryness route contains an explicit negative result that the inflammation route does not.
alternativeEtiologiesToRuleOut: Sjogren's syndrome and other autoimmune sialadenitis, in which acinar loss produces a permanent rather than reversible dryness, and which the located instrument review treats as a separate instrument category from both xerostomia and sialadenitis
Medication-induced xerostomia, a reversible cause requiring a medication review before the obstruction is credited with the symptom
Radiation or radioiodine-induced sialadenitis, which the located sialendoscopy study includes as a distinct 35.4 percent subgroup with a different time course and a different reversibility profile

Ductal stenosis without a calculus, which the reviewed chronic sialadenitis cohort found to carry a heavier quality-of-life burden than sialolithiasis and which is a plausible alternative explanation for the same dryness

governanceNotes: D1 batch 84 (2026-09-27): two bounded associations authored in draft quarantine. sialolithiasis is a dental-oral-expansion-wave-7 identity with a single registered incoming edge before this batch, from mucocele, and the located rapid evidence review places mucocele on the SAME obstruction substrate as the calculus rather than downstream of it, so the two edges authored here do not compete with the existing one. xerostomia carried one registered incoming edge before this batch, from salivary-gland-cancer, and the two routes have materially different mechanisms, reversible duct obstruction here versus gland destruction in malignancy, which is the reason the difference is stated on the face of the edge rather than left to the reviewer.

A REVIEWED AND REJECTED ANCHOR IS RECORDED because the rejection changes what this edge may claim. The prospective chronic sialadenitis cohort that compared sialolithiasis against duct stenosis was located, read, and NOT registered as an anchor here, because it compares two causes of obstruction WITHIN patients already diagnosed with chronic sialadenitis and it reports LOWER symptom burden in the sialolithiasis group than in the stenosis group (SPIT 33.3 versus 45.4, P < .013). Registering it would have supported the opposite emphasis, that stones are the mildest obstructive cause rather than a driver of gland inflammation, so its direction is recorded on the face of the edge as a counterweight and as the reason ductal stenosis is named first among the alternatives to rule out.

WEAKNESS DISCLOSED RATHER THAN PADDED: four of the six reference uses across these two edges are narrative synthesis or methodological review class (a rapid evidence review, a monograph chapter, a patient-reported-outcome systematic review, and a management narrative review), and only two are primary prospective cohorts, both single-arm with no comparator. This is the weakest anchor profile in batch 84 and it is disclosed on the face of the edges rather than masked by the mechanistic clarity of the underlying relationship. The sialadenitis edge additionally rests on a primary cohort that EXPRESSLY EXCLUDED patients with acute sialadenitis, so both edges describe the chronic obstructive presentation only and neither supports an acute-inflammation claim.

WITHHELD ROUTES: mucocele as SHARED-SUBSTRATE, the located review naming mucoceles among the same causes of duct obstruction so the arrow runs toward the obstruction from a different cause rather than from the stone. Sjogren-s-syndrome as DIRECTION REVERSAL, since Sjögren's is a cause of sialadenitis rather than a consequence of a calculus, and the catalog carries both identities. dysphagia as EVIDENCE-INSUFFICIENT, the only located anchors being single-case reports of giant sublingual calculi causing dysphagia, which is case-report class for a rare presentation and does not support a general route. salivary-gland-cancer as ZERO RECORD, with no located anchor reporting malignant transformation of a benign calculus. depression and anxiety as WITHHELD on the located NULL: the located chronic obstructive sialadenitis quality-of-life cohort found that LITHIASIS HAD THE LEAST IMPACT ON QUALITY OF LIFE among the obstructive causes examined, below stenosis and below loss of papilla distensibility, which is an explicit null against a mood route from stone disease specifically and is preserved on the record rather than omitted.

A PARALLEL DISCLOSURE CARRIED FROM THE SIALADENITIS FILE: the same cohort found that potentially obstructive entities including eosinophilic sialodochitis, Sjögren's syndrome and radioiodine-induced sialadenitis were associated with a notable loss of quality of life, so the mood burden in this disease group attaches to the non-stone causes rather than to the calculi, and this is the second consecutive batch in which a withheld mood route was driven by a located null rather than by thin evidence.
